endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: D evelopers of autonomous AI systems with clinical applications (screening, diagnosis, treatment) are in the best position to manage issues of liability arising directly from system failure or misdiagnosis and must accept this liability with measures such as maintaining appropriate medical liability insurance and in their agreements with users.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Information about genomics-data ownership and adherence to personal-data-protection legislation need to be properly presented to patients, particularly as patients may receive care from different professionals and institutions along their treatment journey.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Provide all patients, no later than the date of first service delivery, with a comprehensive Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP), including how protected health information (PHI) may be used by AI solutions, in compliance with HIPAA.

endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI

endorsements.quote: We believe that informed consent is much more than a signed form.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations of Using ChatGPT in Health Care
endorsements.quote: Patients should be informed that their data would be used by ChatGPT, and they should be given the opportunity to provide informed consent.

endorsements.quote: Additionally, how user information will be gathered, utilized, and protected ( 62 ) should also be disclosed, presented periodically, and made available whenever requested by the user, similar to Woebot and Wysa ( 2 ).

endorsements.quote: Institutions should also be transparent about how participants’ data is used and stored.

endorsements.quote: This need nurses to be trained to explain how data may be used in AI applications and ensure patients give informed, voluntary consent.

endorsements.quote: In clinical practice, healthcare providers must be transparent about how AI systems utilize patient data and how they are safeguarding it, in order to not betray the trust that patients are placing in the system.

endorsements.quote: Patients must be explicitly informed if their surgical video logs, clinical outcomes, or biological data will be utilized to train proprietary AI models or optimize robotic software [ 1 , 5 ].

endorsements.quote: To overcome this limitation, processors should establish continuous disclosure mechanisms that enable data subjects to understand how their health information is being used throughout the processing lifecycle and make informed decisions based on changes in processing contexts and risk levels.

evidence.outcome: Stated willingness to consent under basic versus expanded technology and data-use disclosures
evidence.effect: Consent was 84 patients (81.6%) with basic information versus 57 patients (55.3%) after disclosure of AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement; comprehension was not measured.
evidence.quote: When provided basic information about the technology ( Figure , A), 84 patients (81.6%) consented; this decreased to 57 patients (55.3%) when details about AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement were disclosed ( Figure , B).

evidence.title: Can I Trust This Chatbot? Assessing User Privacy in AI-Healthcare Chatbot Applications
evidence.outcome: Whether apps informed users of data use through a privacy policy at sign-up
evidence.effect: Half of the 12 apps did not present a privacy policy during sign-up; most policies failed to address data protection measures.

evidence.outcome: Participant desire for information about app privacy features
evidence.effect: Young adults with HIV wanted more reassurance and explanation about the app's privacy features (13 YWH and 5 providers interviewed).

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve guidance documents and commentaries endorse telling patients how AI uses their data, and a HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices offers one existing channel for doing so. The two studies that test disclosure measured willingness to consent and self-disclosure rather than patient understanding or privacy outcomes, and both reported mixed or null results.

perspectives.view: One qualitative study in a real deployment and one simulated study test disclosure. Neither measured comprehension, and their outcomes (stated consent, self-disclosure to an AI therapist) are indirect. With small samples, mixed findings, and non-comparative or simulated designs, certainty that disclosure achieves informed patients is very low.

Half of 12 AI health chatbot apps showed no privacy policy at sign-up, and most policies omitted data protection measures. These findings show that a disclosure gap exists. No study measured whether better notices reduce unauthorized reuse, breaches, or other privacy harms that reach patients.

In one deployment, expanded disclosure about AI features, storage, and corporate involvement changed stated consent, but the study did not check whether patients understood the content. In a VR study of 90 participants, transparency had no significant effect on self-disclosure. The evidence gives little guidance on format, timing, or delivery burden.

The CHAI playbook ties this practice to the HIPAA requirement to provide a Notice of Privacy Practices by the first date of service, updated to describe AI use of protected health information. Health systems can therefore build on an existing legal obligation, although no supplied study evaluates notice revisions of this kind.

Stated consent fell from 81.6% with basic information to 55.3% after expanded disclosure. If this pattern holds in practice, fuller notices may lower participation in AI-enabled services or data reuse programs. Systems should plan for opt-out handling and staff time to answer questions, although the study did not estimate costs.

The drop in consent after fuller disclosure suggests that patients change their decisions when they learn about AI features and corporate involvement. Young adults with HIV said they wanted more explanation and reassurance about app privacy. Both findings indicate that patients value this information when deciding whether to take part.

The only work involving a population with heightened privacy stakes interviewed 13 young adults with HIV and documented the hazard. It did not test a disclosure practice. Neither test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so the effect of written notices on these groups is unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared AI-specific privacy notices against standard notices on patient comprehension, recall, or opt-out behavior in a real care setting. Trials should measure understanding with validated instruments, test plain-language and translated formats, and track downstream privacy complaints or data-use incidents.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study testing disclosure reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. One test enrolled German mental health patients and the other enrolled U.S. patients without reported insurance or literacy data. Written notices depend on reading ability and language access, so the effect on these groups remains untested and may differ from the reported results.
